# Purnendu Dash: full content

Founder and product architect behind MultiVendorX, DualCube and VuloLabs, building eCommerce and eLearning software on WordPress and WooCommerce.

I'm a product founder and system builder. I work at the intersection of ecommerce, marketplace platforms, and learning management systems, designing practical, scalable solutions for real operational problems.

I lead product and engineering for MultiVendorX, a marketplace platform for WooCommerce. I care about customer service, clean systems, and building software that removes friction instead of adding it.

Principle: Reduce complexity for the customer by solving deep system-level problems with clean, reliable product design.

## Portfolio

- eCommerce (since 2015): MultiVendorX, CatalogX, Notifima. Marketplace and store software for WooCommerce: vendors, commissions, quotes, and stock alerts, without the spreadsheet.
- eLearning (since 2011): DualCube, MooWoodle. Learning platforms that connect courses to commerce, on WordPress and Moodle.
- VuloLabs ecosystem (now, with ai): VuloMail, VuloPilot, VuloForm. AI-powered software and WordPress innovation.

## Product case notes

### MultiVendorX

A WooCommerce-based marketplace ecosystem that removes the operational complexity of running multi-vendor ecommerce businesses.

Problems it addresses:
- Complexity of managing multiple vendors on a single platform
- Lack of flexible, transparent commission systems
- Inefficient order and fulfillment workflows
- Difficulty scaling WooCommerce into true marketplace infrastructure

What it delivers:
- A modular marketplace engine built on WooCommerce
- Flexible commission and revenue-sharing system
- Vendor-first operational workflows
- Extensible architecture for integrations and scaling

### CatalogX

A catalog and quote management layer for WooCommerce stores that need to sell without fixed pricing: request-a-quote, hidden pricing, and B2B catalogs.

Problems it addresses:
- Stores that need catalogs instead of instant checkout
- B2B pricing that isn't meant to be public
- No built-in way to convert enquiries into orders

What it delivers:
- Catalog-mode storefronts with optional hidden pricing
- Request-a-quote workflows built for WooCommerce
- Smooth path from enquiry to order

### Notifima

A stock and price alert system for WooCommerce, keeping customers and store owners informed without manual follow-up.

Problems it addresses:
- Lost sales from out-of-stock products
- No automated way to notify customers when items return
- Manual, ad-hoc customer follow-up

What it delivers:
- Automated back-in-stock and price-drop notifications
- Configurable alerts across email and other channels
- Reduced manual support overhead for store owners

### DualCube

Learning management solutions that help businesses and educators deliver, manage, and monetize digital learning within WordPress and Moodle ecosystems.

Problems it addresses:
- Disconnected learning and ecommerce systems limiting scalability
- Complex, inefficient course creation and management
- Limited flexibility in monetizing and packaging learning content

What it delivers:
- Structured, scalable learning platforms built on WordPress
- Seamless integration of learning with commerce: sell, deliver, and track in one flow
- Robust systems for course delivery, enrollment, and learner lifecycle

## Technology Advisory

Part-time senior technical leadership. Areas covered:

- Technical strategy: Decide what to build, what to buy, and what to leave alone, tied to the business plan rather than the latest tool.
- Architecture: Data models, extension points, and the logic for commissions or enrollment, designed so the product can grow without rewrites.
- Product and roadmap: Turn customer problems into a sequenced roadmap the team can actually ship.
- Team and process: Hiring bar, code review, release process, and how engineers and product people work together.
- Reliability and upkeep: Compatibility, security updates, support load, and the long-term maintenance a plugin or open source product needs.
- AI adoption: Where AI lowers the cost of building or serving customers, and where it adds risk for no gain.

### What is technology advisory?

Senior technical leadership for a company's product and team, on a part-time basis: technical direction, architecture, roadmap, hiring, and AI decisions, without the cost and commitment of a full-time executive.

### How is this different from consulting?

A consultant delivers a report and leaves. Advisory stays accountable for ongoing decisions and the people making them, week after week, until the team can carry on alone.

### Which companies is it for?

Early and growing companies that have a product or a plan but no senior technical leader. Marketplaces, learning platforms, and WordPress or WooCommerce based businesses are the closest fit, because that is where the experience is deepest.

### How do engagements work?

The shape is agreed per company after an initial conversation: how much time, what to focus on, and for how long. There are no fixed packages.

### Can we talk before committing to anything?

Yes. Send a short note about what you are building on the contact page. The first conversation is simply about whether it is a good fit.

## Articles

### Why most WooCommerce marketplaces get vendor payouts wrong

Published August 4, 2026 · Marketplaces, WooCommerce
URL: https://purnendudash.com/blog/vendor-payouts-woocommerce-marketplaces

Most WooCommerce stores start as a single-vendor shop. The moment a second vendor joins, payouts become the hardest problem in the system.

#### Why a flat commission rate breaks

A flat commission rate feels simple at first. It breaks down fast once vendors sell different product categories, run promotions, or need different payout schedules. Stores that hardcode a single rate end up rebuilding their commission logic within a year.

#### Treat commission as a rule engine

The fix is to treat commission as a rule engine, not a number. Rules should apply by vendor, by category, and by product, with a clear order of precedence. Refunds, partial refunds, and disputed orders need their own payout logic too, since they touch money that has often already left the platform.

#### Payout scheduling is the second failure point

Payout scheduling is the second failure point. Vendors expect predictable payment dates, not a manual process the store owner runs when they remember to. Automating payout runs, even on a simple weekly schedule, removes a huge amount of support overhead.

This is the core problem MultiVendorX was built to solve: giving store owners a flexible, rule-based commission and payout system instead of a single hardcoded percentage.

### LMS and ecommerce do not have to be separate systems

Published June 18, 2026 · LMS, Ecommerce
URL: https://purnendudash.com/blog/lms-and-ecommerce-dont-have-to-be-separate

A business selling courses usually ends up running two systems side by side: a store to take payment, and an LMS to deliver the content. Connecting them is often an afterthought, handled with a plugin or a manual export.

#### What the split looks like to a learner

The result is a learner experience with gaps. A student pays, then waits for enrollment to sync. A refund happens on the store side but access is not revoked on the LMS side. Reporting lives in two places that do not agree with each other.

#### Design learning and commerce as one system

Designing learning and commerce as one system from the start avoids this. Enrollment should be a direct result of a completed order, not a separate step. Access, refunds, and reporting should read from the same source of truth.

This is the problem DualCube focuses on: building WordPress and Moodle based learning platforms where commerce and course delivery are part of the same workflow, not two systems bolted together.

### Fifteen years of building an open source WordPress plugin

Published April 22, 2026 · Open Source, WordPress
URL: https://purnendudash.com/blog/fifteen-years-open-source-wordpress-plugin

MultiVendorX started in 2015 as a small plugin to help one WooCommerce store manage a handful of vendors. It has since grown alongside WordPress itself, through major WooCommerce rewrites and years of core releases.

#### Backward compatibility is a feature

The biggest lesson has been that backward compatibility is a feature, not an afterthought. Store owners do not upgrade everything at once. A plugin has to work across a wide range of WordPress and WooCommerce versions at the same time.

#### Community support shaped the product

Community support shaped the product more than any roadmap document. Forum threads and support tickets surface real operational problems long before they show up in a feature request. Some of the most useful features in MultiVendorX came directly from a support conversation.

#### What contributing to core changed

Contributing to WordPress core, through releases like 5.1 and 4.9, also changed how I build plugins. Seeing how core decisions get made makes it easier to build products that respect the platform instead of fighting it.

Fifteen years in, the plugin looks nothing like it did in 2015. The principle behind it has not changed: reduce operational complexity for the store owner, one release at a time.

### A founder's guide to multi-vendor commission models

Published February 11, 2026 · Marketplaces, Strategy
URL: https://purnendudash.com/blog/founders-guide-multi-vendor-commission-models

Founders often start a marketplace by picking a commission percentage and moving on. That decision deserves more attention, because it directly shapes which vendors want to join the platform.

#### Why a flat percentage rarely stays fair

A flat percentage is easy to explain but rarely fair across categories. A vendor selling low-margin goods and a vendor selling high-margin goods should not pay the same rate if the platform wants both to stay.

#### Tiered commissions reward your best vendors

Tiered commissions, where the rate drops as a vendor's sales volume grows, reward your best vendors and give newer ones an incentive to grow on your platform instead of leaving.

#### Category-based commissions price risk and effort

Category-based commissions let a marketplace price risk and effort differently. Categories with high return rates or high support costs can carry a different rate than low-maintenance categories.

Whatever model a founder chooses, it needs to be visible to vendors and easy to change without a developer. Commission logic that lives only in code, instead of in settings vendors and admins can see, becomes a support burden the moment the business needs to adjust it.

### Speaking at WordCamp: lessons from organizing and presenting

Published November 30, 2025 · Speaking, Community
URL: https://purnendudash.com/blog/speaking-at-wordcamp-lessons

Organizing a WordCamp gives you a very different view of the WordPress community than speaking at one. As an organizer, you see how much volunteer effort goes into a single day of talks, from venue logistics to reviewing every session proposal.

#### Talk about the problem, not the plugin

As a speaker, the biggest lesson has been to talk less about the plugin and more about the problem. A room full of store owners and developers does not need a feature tour. They need to see themselves in the problem before they care about the solution.

#### The best questions come after the talk

The best questions after a talk are rarely about the product itself. They are about a specific operational headache the attendee is dealing with right now. Preparing to answer those, not just to deliver slides, is what makes a WordCamp talk useful instead of just a demo.

Community events like WordCamp are also where a lot of real product feedback happens, in hallway conversations that never make it into a support ticket.
